university: California Polytechnic State University, San Luis Obispo

documents.title: Syllabus Statements: AI Core Values and Syllabus Statements
documents.summary: The CTLT page gives Cal Poly faculty core-value statements and sample syllabus statements in three categories (prohibited, restricted, permitted and encouraged) to copy or adapt. It sets no campus-wide stance and leaves the choice to each instructor, while tying misuse to the Academic Integrity Policy.
documents.stance_why: The page says "Please edit and adapt any of the following examples at your discretion" and offers three template categories ("If AI use is prohibited", "restricted or limited", "permitted and encouraged"), so it hands the decision to instructors and lists tiers rather than setting one rule.

units.why: The page invites faculty to adapt the sample statements "at your discretion", so each instructor sets the AI rule; P04 fits rather than P09 because it permits choice instead of requiring a statement.
units.anchor: Please edit and adapt any of the following examples at your discretion.

units.why: The page says its resources "are intended to support the development of transparent classroom policies and encourage thoughtful decisions to use, or not use AI"; this states the purpose of the resources and leaves use or non-use to each instructor, so informs under P04 (who decides).
units.anchor: encourage thoughtful decisions to use, or not use AI in teaching strategies and course design
units.policy: Resources support instructors in making thoughtful decisions to use, or not use, AI in teaching strategies and course design.
units.resolution_why: A coded should, B coded informs; both P04, instructor, before-course. The sentence describes what the resources are intended to do and does not tell instructors to do anything, so informs.

units.why: Syllabus statements are justified as a way to "reduce students' uncertainty" and set expectations at the outset; this explains why AI expectations are communicated early, so it goes under communicating expectations (P09) as informs.
units.anchor: help establish students' expectations about the course at the outset

units.why: The page points faculty to CSU AI Commons guidance, a support resource for instructors writing AI policy; P63 (support faculty in learning AI) is the closest type.
units.anchor: official guidance from the CSU system on incorporating AI in instruction
units.resolution_why: A coded P63 (support for faculty), B coded P56 (institution-wide framework). The sentence points faculty to CSU AI Commons guidance as a place to start when writing course AI policy; that is a resource for faculty learning about AI in instruction (P63), not an institutional framework of this campus.

units.why: The page sorts sample statements into three named categories ("If AI use is prohibited", "restricted or limited", "permitted and encouraged"), which is a tiered scheme (P05).
units.anchor: If AI use is restricted or limited
units.policy: The page offers sample syllabus statements in three categories: AI use prohibited, AI use restricted or limited, and AI permitted and encouraged.
units.resolution_why: Only A coded this heading as a tier scheme. The page sorts its sample statements into three named categories (prohibited / restricted or limited / permitted and encouraged), which is P05; kept.

units.why: "Consider including core values ... in your syllabus" recommends instructors put a values statement in the syllabus; "should" because it is a suggestion, and P09 covers syllabus statements.
units.anchor: Consider including core values for student use of AI in your syllabus
units.resolution_why: Only A coded this. "Consider including core values for student use of AI in your syllabus" is a real recommendation to instructors, kept.

units.why: "any syllabi statements on AI usage should align with Cal Poly's policies on Academic Integrity" ties instructor statements to the university integrity framework; P56 fits better than P36 because the sentence classifies no misuse and names no sanction.
units.anchor: any syllabi statements on AI usage should align with Cal Poly’s policies on Academic Integrity
units.resolution_why: A coded P36, B coded P56. The source only tells instructors to align syllabus statements with the Academic Integrity policy; it does not classify misuse as misconduct, so P56 (institution-level framework) is the closer fit.

units.why: Core value Integrity says "Use AI tools to support learning, not to circumvent academic responsibilities", limiting AI to learning support; P41 (AI as shortcut undermines learning) fits better than P19 because it is about purpose, not output.
units.anchor: Use AI tools to support learning, not to circumvent academic responsibilities.
units.resolution_why: Same type and codes; topics differed (B used permitted-uses). Kept learning-rationale and accountability-understanding.

units.why: Students are told to "Distinguish your own original work by properly acknowledging all AI-generated content", an acknowledgment duty, so P24.
units.anchor: properly acknowledging all AI-generated content

units.why: Transparency value: "Be clear and honest about when and how AI tools have been used in your work" is a disclosure duty (P24).
units.anchor: Be clear and honest about when and how AI tools have been used

units.why: "Disclose AI assistance in line with institutional guidelines" explicitly asks for disclosure (P24); it is a separate sentence from the general honesty value above.
units.anchor: Disclose AI assistance in line with institutional guidelines.

units.why: The example "This essay was drafted with the assistance of ChatGPT and edited for originality" models a disclosure statement; it names the tool, so P25 fits better than P24.
units.anchor: This essay was drafted with the assistance of ChatGPT and edited for originality.
units.resolution_why: Only B coded this. The example in the Transparency value models a disclosure statement that names the tool; it illustrates the disclosure duty and is kept as P25 (cites the tool), informs.

units.why: Accountability value "Always verify the accuracy and reliability of AI-generated information" tells students to check AI output (P31).
units.anchor: Always verify the accuracy and reliability of AI-generated information
units.resolution_why: A coded should, B coded must. The core-value statements are offered as samples that the instructor may include ("Consider including core values") and every other value is coded should; a student-facing 'Always verify' value is a recommendation here, so should.

units.why: "you are ultimately responsible for the quality and originality of your submissions" makes students own what they submit (P29).
units.anchor: you are ultimately responsible for the quality and originality of your submissions
units.resolution_why: Phase differed: A general, B during-work. "Recognize that you are ultimately responsible" is a general principle for all AI use rather than an act at a particular stage, so general.

units.why: "Treat AI-generated suggestions as starting points, not final answers" keeps the student as thinker, so P32 rather than P31, which is about checking correctness.
units.anchor: Treat AI-generated suggestions as starting points, not final answers.
units.resolution_why: unit_stance differed (A restrict, B permit). Treating suggestions "as starting points" accepts AI suggestions as input to the student's own work, so permit.

units.why: "AI tools may generate inaccurate or biased information" warns that AI output can be wrong or biased (P31).
units.anchor: AI tools may generate inaccurate or biased information.
units.resolution_why: A coded informs/general, B coded should/during-work. "Recognize that AI tools may generate inaccurate or biased information" states a fact about AI output; informs, general. P31 kept (B also P31).

units.why: "Apply your own analysis, reasoning, and creativity to refine AI outputs" has students keep doing the thinking (P32).
units.anchor: Apply your own analysis, reasoning, and creativity to refine AI outputs.
units.resolution_why: unit_stance differed (A neutral, B permit). Refining AI outputs with one's own analysis assumes AI output is used, so permit.

units.why: Among the "when in doubt" questions, asking whether the student has "discussed how AI should and not be used" with the instructor tells unsure students to consult the instructor (P10).
units.anchor: Have I discussed how AI should and not be used for learning
units.resolution_why: Only topics differed. Dropped prohibited-uses (not in the sentence).

units.why: The question "as a tool to learn and create or as a shortcut to avoid effort?" frames AI as acceptable if it does not bypass effort; P41 (shortcuts the practice that builds skill).
units.anchor: as a tool to learn and create or as a shortcut to avoid effort?

units.why: "Would I be comfortable explaining how I used AI to my instructor or peers?" is a test pointing toward openness about AI use; P24 is the nearest type, not P30, since it concerns how AI was used rather than understanding of the work.
units.anchor: Would I be comfortable explaining how I used AI to my instructor or peers?
units.resolution_why: A coded P24 (disclosure), B coded P30 (explain every line). The question is about being comfortable explaining how AI was used, which is openness about use rather than understanding of the submitted work, so P24.

units.why: "Does this use align with my institution's academic integrity policies?" tells students to check their use against integrity rules; P56 as an institutional framework pointer.
units.anchor: Does this use align with my institution's academic integrity policies?
units.resolution_why: Only B coded this. The gray-area question tells students to check use against integrity policies; coded P56 like the instruction to align syllabus statements with the Academic Integrity policy.

units.why: Prohibition example 1 states AI use "is strictly prohibited in this course", a default ban on the course work (P01).
units.anchor: is strictly prohibited in this course
units.resolution_why: Phase differed: A during-work, B course-start. The sentence bans AI use on the course's work, which acts on students while they do the work, so during-work.

units.why: "All assignments, essays, and other submitted work must be your original, independent creation" requires submitted work to be the student's own (P29).
units.anchor: must be your original, independent creation

units.why: "submitting AI-generated work will be considered a violation of the Cal Poly Academic Integrity Policy" classifies it as misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: submitting AI-generated work will be considered a violation of the Cal Poly

units.why: "may result in a failing grade for the assignment or the course" names a concrete penalty, so P37.
units.anchor: may result in a failing grade for the assignment or the course

units.why: Prohibition example 2 says "you may not use them in this course", a default ban (P01).
units.anchor: you may not use them in this course
units.resolution_why: Phase differed (A during-work, B course-start); the ban governs students' work, so during-work.

units.why: "you should not use generative AI to write, outline, revise, or polish any part of your assignments" bans AI producing the submitted work; chosen P19 because writing and outlining dominate, though revise/polish touches P21.
units.anchor: you should not use generative AI to write, outline, revise, or polish any part
units.resolution_why: Modality: A must-not, B should-not. The source wording is "you should not", but it follows "you may not use them in this course" and "This means", so it is the ban itself: must-not. Topics: writing-assistance fits better than code-generation because the example is a non-coding course with essays and assignments.

units.why: "When you submit your work, you're affirming that it's your own original creation" states students own their submissions (P29).
units.anchor: you're affirming that it's your own original creation
units.resolution_why: Only B coded this. "When you submit your work, you're affirming that it's your own original creation" is the ownership duty (P29), stated as informs; kept.

units.why: "it will be addressed according to the university's academic integrity policies" sends inappropriate AI use to the integrity process (P36).
units.anchor: it will be addressed according to the university’s academic integrity policies

units.why: "I'm here to support your growth, and that starts with honest, authentic work" gives a learning/honesty rationale for the ban (P41).
units.anchor: that starts with honest, authentic work
units.resolution_why: Only B coded this. "I'm here to support your growth, and that starts with honest, authentic work" gives the rationale for the ban (learning and honesty, P41), informs; kept.

units.why: "may only be used for specific purposes and assignments ... as explicitly authorized by me" permits AI only for uses the instructor authorizes; the permission is the may, and the ban on everything else is the next unit. P04 because the instructor decides per assignment (P06 is for silent syllabi, P01 would ignore the permission).
units.anchor: may only be used for specific purposes and assignments
units.resolution_why: A coded must-not, B coded may; both P04. The sentence grants a narrow permission for authorized uses, and the prohibition on all other uses is a separate sentence coded in the next unit, so may.

units.why: "You may not, however, use these technologies for any other assignments or aspects of this course" bans AI outside the authorized uses, a course default ban (P01); P06 does not fit because it is not about a silent syllabus.
units.anchor: You may not, however, use these technologies for any other assignments
units.resolution_why: A coded P01, B coded P06 (fallback when syllabus is silent). The sentence bans all uses the instructor has not authorized in an explicit statement; it does not address a silent syllabus, so P01. unit_stance prohibit since the sentence itself is a ban.

units.why: "Any use of authorized AI-generated content must be documented and cited" requires acknowledgment (P24).
units.anchor: must be documented and cited according to
units.resolution_why: Only anchor wording differed; same codes.

units.why: "If you are unsure of how to use or cite AI in this course appropriately, please ask me" tells unsure students to ask (P10).
units.anchor: unsure of how to use or cite AI in this course appropriately, please ask me
units.resolution_why: Phase differed: A during-work, B course-start. The student asks when unsure how to use or cite AI in the course, which happens while working, so during-work.

units.why: "Unauthorized use of AI in this course is a violation of the Cal Poly Academic Integrity policy and will be treated as plagiarism" makes misuse misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: Unauthorized use of AI in this course is a violation

units.why: "Violations may result in a failing grade for the assignment or the course" gives a concrete penalty (P37) in the restricted template.
units.anchor: Violations may result in a failing grade for the assignment or the course.

units.why: "You are welcome to use generative AI tools ... in this class as doing so aligns with the course objectives of Creating Mission and Vision Statements, Creating a Sample Budget, and Creating Plans" permits AI for the named assignments only, a per-assignment rule (P04), may; the sentence itself permits use.
units.anchor: You are welcome to use generative AI tools
units.policy: Students are welcome to use generative AI tools in this class as doing so aligns with the course objectives of Creating Mission and Vision Statements, Creating a Sample Budget, and Creating Plans for their own Performing Arts Organization or Museum.
units.resolution_why: unit_stance differed (A permit, B restrict) and phase (during-work vs course-start). The sentence welcomes AI for named assignments, so permit; the matching ban on remaining assignments is coded in the next unit. Used B's anchor and a normalized policy.

units.why: "You may not use generative AI for the remaining assignments" bans AI on all other assignments; coded P01 as the ban, since the preceding unit already carries the per-assignment permission (P04).
units.anchor: You may not use generative AI for the remaining assignments.
units.resolution_why: A coded P01, B coded P04. The sentence is the ban on every assignment not named in the previous sentence; the per-assignment permission is carried by the previous unit, so this one is P01, a default ban for the remainder.

units.why: "You are responsible for the information you submit based on an AI query" makes students own submitted content (P29); the IP and misinformation examples are secondary.
units.anchor: You are responsible for the information you submit based on an AI query
units.resolution_why: unit_stance differed (A neutral, B restrict). The sentence assigns responsibility and takes no position on AI use itself, so neutral.

units.why: "must be properly documented and cited in order to stay within university policies" requires citation (P24).
units.anchor: Your use of AI tools must be properly documented and cited
units.resolution_why: unit_stance differed (A permit, B restrict). The sentence sits in the restricted template and conditions allowed use on documentation, so restrict, consistent with the same duty in restricted example 1.

units.why: "AI is not likely to generate a response that would be seen as quality work and should be modified and improved" tells students not to take AI output as is (P31).
units.anchor: should be modified and improved
units.resolution_why: unit_stance differed (A neutral, B restrict). It tells students to improve AI output and takes no position on whether AI may be used, so neutral.

units.why: "you are welcome to use generative AI tools ... and in some cases, you will be expected to do so" welcomes and sometimes expects AI (P02).
units.anchor: and in some cases, you will be expected to do so
units.resolution_why: Phase differed: A during-work, B course-start. The sentence tells students what use is welcome/expected in the course; as a rule on doing the work, during-work.

units.why: "AI usage should be documented and cited" sets a citation duty in the permissive template (P24).
units.anchor: AI usage should be documented and cited

units.why: "ensuring that any information generated by AI is accurate and ethical" makes students check AI output (P31); the IP duty in the same sentence is coded separately.
units.anchor: ensuring that any information generated by AI is accurate and ethical
units.resolution_why: Only A coded this separately. B folded it into the IP unit. "ensuring that any information generated by AI is accurate and ethical" is a distinct verification duty from the IP duty, so kept as its own P31 unit.

units.why: "responsible for respecting intellectual property" is an IP duty for AI use (P52).
units.anchor: responsible for respecting intellectual property

units.why: Permitted example 2 says "you are welcome to use generative artificial intelligence (AI) models", a permissive default (P02).
units.anchor: you are welcome to use generative artificial intelligence (AI) models
units.resolution_why: Phase differed (A during-work, B course-start); during-work for the same reason as the other default-use rules.

units.why: "with correct acknowledgment (you can ask the AI to cite itself in APA7" conditions use on acknowledgment (P24).
units.anchor: with correct acknowledgment (you can ask the AI to cite itself in APA7
units.resolution_why: A coded P24, B coded P25 for the parenthetical. "you can ask the AI to cite itself in APA7" is a way to acknowledge AI use and does not require tool, prompt or output details, so P24 (acknowledge) not P25.

units.why: The statement warns models "tend to locate incorrect facts and submit them as fact", a note that AI output is often wrong (P31).
units.anchor: tend to locate incorrect facts and submit them as fact
units.resolution_why: Only A coded the incorrect-facts clause separately; B folded it into the bias/harms unit. The clause warns that models submit incorrect facts as fact, a distinct point (P31) from bias and harms, so kept.

units.why: The same sentence names harms ("perpetuate biases, create offensive products"), so P53 (bias and harms).
units.anchor: perpetuate biases, create offensive products, and may violate copyright
units.resolution_why: Phase differed: A general, B during-work. The warning that models make errors and perpetuate biases is background information, so general. A also coded the incorrect-facts clause as a separate P31 unit (kept, see next).

units.why: "be sure that you consider ethical AI usage, data privacy and security, addressing potential biases" tells students to weigh ethics and privacy; P53 chosen for the ethics and bias focus, with privacy as a topic.
units.anchor: consider ethical AI usage, data privacy and security, addressing potential biases in AI algorithms
units.resolution_why: unit_stance differed (A neutral, B permit). It asks students to consider ethics and privacy and does not take a stance on whether AI is used, so neutral.

units.why: "you will be responsible for any inaccurate, biased, offensive, or unethical content you submit, regardless of its origin" makes students own all submitted content (P29).
units.anchor: responsible for any inaccurate, biased, offensive, or unethical content you submit
units.resolution_why: unit_stance differed (A neutral, B permit); responsibility for submitted content takes no stance on AI use, so neutral.

units.why: "Any use of AI-generated content must be documented and cited" repeats the citation duty in the second permitted example; coded because each example is a stand-alone template (P24).
units.anchor: Any use of AI-generated content must be documented and cited according to

units.why: "AI tools should support, not replace, your learning" is an optional addition keeping the student as the learner and thinker (P32).
units.anchor: AI tools should support, not replace, your learning.
units.resolution_why: Same codes. B anchored the second sentence of Addition #1 ("AI should enhance learning, not substitute critical thinking"); the two sentences state one rule, so one unit with A's anchor.

units.why: "Use of AI is entirely voluntary and optional" makes AI optional for students, an access and equity style provision (P51).
units.anchor: Use of AI is entirely voluntary and optional.
units.resolution_why: Phase differed (A during-work, B course-start); kept during-work.

units.why: "you must accurately cite your AI use" is a required citation (P24).
units.anchor: you must accurately cite your AI use
units.resolution_why: B merged this citation duty with the prompt questions into one P25 unit; kept as a separate P24 unit (see the P25 unit that follows).

units.why: The addition asks students to answer "What was your prompt?" and about follow-up questions, so the citation includes prompt details (P25).
units.anchor: include answers to the following questions: What was your prompt?
units.resolution_why: A split the sentence into a citation duty (P24) and a prompt/output details duty (P25); B merged them as one P25 unit with a long policy. They are two distinct rules, so both are kept; B's unit is matched to the P25 part.

documents.title: Course Syllabi (academic policy)
documents.summary: The campus syllabus policy lists the minimum content of a syllabus, one item of which is a course policy on student use of generative AI and other automated systems. It does not say what the policy must be, so the stance is left to each instructor.
documents.stance_why: The only AI provision is the required syllabus item "Course policies governing the student use of generative artificial intelligence and other automated systems"; it requires a statement but sets no stance, so the decision is delegated to instructors.

units.why: The campus syllabus policy lists "Course policies governing the student use of generative artificial intelligence and other automated systems" among what syllabi "shall at minimum include", so every syllabus needs an AI statement (P09); the requirement is about syllabus content, so before-course, not course-start.
units.anchor: Course policies governing the student use of generative artificial intelligence and other automated systems
units.policy: Course syllabi shall at minimum include course policies governing the student use of generative artificial intelligence and other automated systems.
units.resolution_why: Phase differed: A course-start, B before-course. The requirement concerns what the syllabus must contain (course design), so before-course. Used A's full anchor and B's policy wording.

units.why: The footnote says "Some syllabus statements on course policies and use of generative artificial intelligence can be found at" the CTLT page: a pointer to sample statements that helps instructors write the required AI policy, so P63 (support for faculty) rather than P09, which is the requirement itself.
units.anchor: Some syllabus statements on course policies and use of generative artificial intelligence
units.resolution_why: A coded P09, B coded P63. The footnote requires nothing; it points instructors to sample statements, which is support for faculty setting policy (P63).

documents.title: Academic Senate Ad Hoc Committee on Generative Artificial Intelligence
documents.summary: This page describes an ad hoc Academic Senate committee charged to study GAI use, draft guiding principles and integrity principles, and propose resources for faculty and students by the end of AY 2025-26. It is a charge, not a policy, and states no rule on student AI use.
documents.stance_why: The page states a "Rationale" and "Charges" for a committee that will "Formulate general guiding principles" that "should determine specific policies appropriate to their needs"; it sets no stance itself and defers specifics to colleges and divisions.

units.why: The rationale says faculty set "academic standards and safeguards to ensure GAI supports rather than undermines Cal Poly's Learn by Doing mission", a purpose statement for the institution (P56).
units.anchor: ensure GAI supports rather than undermines Cal Poly’s Learn by Doing mission
units.resolution_why: Only anchor/topic wording differed; same codes.

units.why: The committee will "develop a comprehensible, aspirational vision for GAI use at Cal Poly", an institution-level framework (P56).
units.anchor: develop a comprehensible, aspirational vision for GAI use at Cal Poly

units.why: The charge to "Conduct a self-study of GAI use and attitudes at Cal Poly" gathers evidence on AI use (P55).
units.anchor: Conduct a self-study of GAI use and attitudes at Cal Poly.

units.why: "Produce a concise brief tracking trends in GAI use in higher education and industry" collects evidence on AI use (P55).
units.anchor: Produce a concise brief tracking trends in GAI use in higher education and industry

units.why: The committee is to "Formulate general guiding principles concerning GAI use at Cal Poly", an institution-wide framework (P56).
units.anchor: Formulate general guiding principles concerning GAI use at Cal Poly

units.why: The principles "should determine specific policies appropriate to their needs" in colleges and divisions, delegating specifics (P04).
units.anchor: which should determine specific policies appropriate to their needs
units.resolution_why: Only A coded this as a separate unit; B's guiding-principles unit extends to "policies appropriate to their needs" and folds it in. The principles "should determine specific policies appropriate to their needs" in colleges and divisions is a distinct delegation rule (P04), so kept.

units.why: "resources for how to advance GAI literacy for both faculty and students" is about supporting AI learning; P63 chosen because it covers faculty, with student literacy in the same charge.
units.anchor: resources for how to advance GAI literacy for both faculty and students

units.why: "support GAI-literate faculty adopters and abstainers" supports faculty whether or not they use AI in teaching (P63).
units.anchor: support GAI-literate faculty adopters and abstainers of the use of GAI in teaching

units.why: "Formulate general principles of academic integrity with respect to GAI use" sets up integrity principles; P56 (framework) chosen because no misconduct rule is stated yet.
units.anchor: Formulate general principles of academic integrity with respect to GAI use

units.why: Charge to "provide guidelines to distinguish ethical and unethical uses of GAI by both faculty and students" is a framework on responsible use (P56).
units.anchor: Provide guidelines to distinguish ethical and unethical uses of GAI by both faculty and students.
units.resolution_why: Only B coded this. The sentence says the planned ethical-use guidelines would address privacy, data security, bias, accessibility, copyright/IP, disclosure and responsible research/creative practice. It is part of the charge in the same way as the neighboring items, so kept as P56 informs.

units.why: "Review and make some recommendations on the use of specific GAI technologies at Cal Poly (e.g., ChatGPT.edu)" concerns which tools are vetted for campus use (P50).
units.anchor: Review and make some recommendations on the use of specific GAI technologies at Cal Poly

units.why: The guidelines "would address issues such as privacy, data security, bias, accessibility, copyright/IP, disclosure, and responsible research/creative practice", listing responsible-use concerns planned for coverage (P56).
units.anchor: privacy, data security, bias, accessibility, copyright/IP, disclosure, and responsible research/creative practice
units.resolution_why: Only B coded this; it lists the issues the planned ethical-use guidelines would address. Kept as P56 informs, in line with the neighboring charge items.

notes: Course layer deferred; no school or computing-unit AI policy found. The Senate page is a committee charge listing planned work, coded as P55/P56/P63 for planning statements; it is not a policy. Template examples on the CTLT page contain bracketed placeholders. Source for the syllabus requirement: Academic Senate Resolution AS 1011-26 (approved 28 July 2026). calpoly-ctlt-resources was screened out in collection and not coded. Reconciled from coders A and B.
